assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Cryolite
items.clue: The compound mixed with aluminium oxide in the aluminium cell.

items.label: Inert electrode
items.clue: An electrode, such as graphite or platinum, that does not take part in the reactions of the cell, so the products come only from the electrolyte.

items.label: Hypothesis
items.clue: A testable idea, put forward before the experiment, that predicts what will happen and can be supported or disproved by the results of Required practical 3.

items.label: Electrolysis
items.clue: The process in which passing an electric current through an electrolyte makes the ions move to the electrodes, where they are discharged to produce elements.

questions.stem: Molten lead bromide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. What is produced at the cathode?

options.text: Bromine, because the non-metals form there
Lead, the metal, collects at the cathode
Hydrogen, made from water in this melt
Lead ions, Pb²⁺, coating the whole electrode

questions.explanation: Lead ions are positive, so they move to the negative electrode and are discharged as lead metal.

questions.stem: When an aqueous solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes, what decides which ions are discharged?

options.text: The size of the charge carried by each of the ions
The mass of each of the ions present in the solution
The metal is discharged whatever else is there
The relative reactivity of the elements involved

questions.explanation: The specification states that the ions discharged depend on the relative reactivity of the elements involved.

questions.stem: Copper chloride solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the cathode?

options.text: Hydrogen, because copper is less reactive than it
Copper, as it is less reactive than hydrogen
Chlorine, since chloride ions are drawn there
Oxygen, released as the water breaks apart

questions.explanation: The less reactive element is discharged, and copper is below hydrogen in reactivity.

questions.stem: Sodium sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the cathode?

options.text: Sodium, because it is the metal in the compound used
Sulfur, which forms from the sulfate ions in solution
Hydrogen, as sodium is more reactive than hydrogen
Oxygen, which the water always gives off there

questions.explanation: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen ions from the water are discharged instead.

questions.stem: Sodium chloride solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the anode?

options.text: Sodium, which is drawn to the positive electrode
Hydrogen, coming from the water in the solution
Oxygen, which always forms at that electrode
Chlorine, as the solution holds halide ions

questions.explanation: Oxygen is produced at the anode unless the solution contains halide ions, when the halogen is produced.

questions.stem: Copper sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the anode?

options.text: Oxygen, as no halide ions are present
Sulfur dioxide, made from the sulfate ions
Copper, plating onto the positive electrode
Hydrogen, from the breakdown of the water

questions.explanation: Sulfate is not a halide, so hydroxide ions from the water are discharged and oxygen is produced.

questions.stem: In the electrolysis of an aqueous solution, where do the hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions come from?

options.text: From the dissolved compound splitting into its ions
From water molecules that break down in the solution
From hydrogen and oxygen gas dissolved in water
From the electrodes, which release them into the liquid

questions.explanation: In the aqueous solution water molecules break down producing hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions.

questions.stem: A student plans Required practical 3 and writes an idea down before starting. Which statement is a hypothesis the investigation could test?

options.text: Copper chloride solution is a clear blue liquid
Bubbles appeared at the negative electrode
Solutions of halides will give a halogen at the anode
Which gas is given off at the negative electrode?

questions.explanation: It is a testable prediction, made in advance, that the results of the practical can support or disprove.

questions.stem: In Required practical 3, the gas collected at the cathode gave a squeaky pop with a lit splint. What does this show?

options.text: Hydrogen formed, so the metal is more reactive
Oxygen formed, because oxygen relights the splint
Chlorine formed, since it bleaches damp litmus paper
The metal itself formed and burned with the lit splint

questions.explanation: A squeaky pop identifies hydrogen, which is discharged when the metal is more reactive than hydrogen.

questions.stem: Molten lead bromide is electrolysed. Which half equation shows the reaction at the cathode?

options.text: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb
Pb²⁺ + e⁻ → Pb
2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻
2Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2Pb

questions.explanation: Each lead ion carries two positive charges, so it gains two electrons at the cathode to form a lead atom.

questions.stem: Sodium chloride solution is electrolysed. Which half equation shows the reaction at the anode?

options.text: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
2Cl⁻ + 2e⁻ → Cl₂
2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 4e⁻
2Na⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2Na

questions.explanation: Two chloride ions each lose one electron at the anode, giving one molecule of chlorine; atoms and charge balance.

questions.stem: At the cathode, positively charged ions gain electrons. How is this reaction described?

options.text: Oxidation, because the electrons are gained
Reduction, because electrons are gained
Oxidation, as the cathode is negative
Neutralisation, as the charge has gone

questions.explanation: Reduction is gain of electrons, so reactions at the cathode are reductions.

questions.stem: At the anode, negatively charged ions lose electrons. How is this reaction described?

options.text: Reduction, because electrons are lost
Reduction, since the anode is positive
Oxidation, as electrons are lost by the ions
Oxidation, because oxygen is always made here

questions.explanation: Oxidation is loss of electrons, so reactions at the anode are oxidations.

questions.stem: Which pair of half equations represents the reactions at the two electrodes correctly?

options.text: 2H⁺ → H₂ + 2e⁻ at the cathode and 4OH⁻ + 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O at the anode
H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂ at the cathode and OH⁻ → O₂ + H₂O + e⁻ at the anode
4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ at the cathode, 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ at the anode
2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ at the cathode, and 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ at the anode

questions.explanation: Positive ions gain electrons at the cathode and negative ions lose electrons at the anode; both equations balance.

questions.stem: Which half equation shows hydrogen being produced at the cathode?

options.text: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂
2H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂
H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂

questions.explanation: Two hydrogen ions gain two electrons to form one molecule of hydrogen; atoms and charge both balance.
